metadata.title: Take the Test: Sample Questions from OECD’s PISA Assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD volume is a compilation of publicly released PISA sample questions and scoring information, not an analysis of student microdata. It describes how PISA is administered (randomly selected schools, booklets of units, and a two-hour test plus a student questionnaire) and how responses are scored using detailed scoring guides. Because no empirical modeling or estimation is conducted here, there is no reported use of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures. For any future secondary analysis using PISA microdata, analysts should apply the official sampling/survey weights provided in the PISA dataset (and replicate weights if available) to account for the multistage sampling design and clustering at school levels.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document does not perform student-level statistical estimation or predictive modeling on PISA achievement outcomes; it presents sample items, their scoring, and general descriptions of PISA administration and proficiency scales. As a result, plausible values (PV-based achievement scores) are not generated or combined, and missing-data handling for PVs is not applicable to the reported content. The only quantitative elements shown are item-level scoring guidance (e.g., difficulty in score points and percent correct across OECD countries) rather than model-based inference requiring PV and missing-data procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: This is not an empirical student-level study. It compiles publicly available PISA questions used in PISA 2000, 2003, and 2006 (and additional questions used in developing and trying out the surveys). The book does not define an analytic subsample of students; instead, it provides item-level scoring guidance and general descriptions of PISA administration (randomly selected schools, two-hour test, and a student questionnaire).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report is a compilation of publicly released PISA sample questions across reading, mathematics, and science, including item-level scoring guidance and (for items used in PISA surveys) information such as percent correct across OECD countries and item difficulty expressed in score points. It explains that PISA assesses 15-year-old students’ literacy in real-life contexts rather than mastery of a specific curriculum, and that tests are administered to students in randomly selected schools using booklet units with multiple response formats. It also describes the three-year cycle of PISA (2000, 2003, 2006) and the use of proficiency scales (e.g., average 500 with two-thirds of students between 400 and 600). The volume does not estimate models or train predictive algorithms; therefore, it provides assessment content and framework context rather than empirical ML results. Country results for the questions are referenced as being available in Annex B.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a framework/content compilation rather than an empirical large-scale assessment analysis. It contains no student-level dataset, no analytic sample definition, and no statistical modeling outputs (e.g., PV estimation, missing-data procedures, or ML performance metrics). Consequently, fields required for empirical ML studies (main_findings, confounders, PV handling details, and missing-data handling) are either empty or set to non-applicable/not reported because the report does not conduct inference.
